body:
Chemical Energy and Electrical Energy

An electric torch produces light even when it is not connected to a power station. It obtains electrical energy from the cells placed inside it. These cells contain substances that undergo chemical reactions and produce an electric current.

An electrochemical cell is a device in which chemical reactions produce electrical energy or electrical energy is used to bring about chemical changes. A cell that produces electrical energy through a spontaneous chemical reaction is called a galvanic or voltaic cell.

An electric cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy. A battery is technically a combination of one or more electrochemical cells arranged to supply electrical energy. In everyday language, even a single packaged cell may be called a battery.

The chemical substances inside a cell possess stored chemical energy. When the cell supplies current to a connected device, chemical reactions convert part of this stored energy into electrical energy. A torch then converts electrical energy into light and heat.

Main Parts of an Electrochemical Cell

A typical cell contains 2 electrodes and an electrolyte. Many modern cells also contain a separator that prevents direct electrical contact between the electrodes while permitting the necessary movement of ions.

  • Electrodes: These are electrically conducting parts where chemical reactions occur. A cell has 2 electrodes connected to its external terminals.
  • Electrolyte: This is a substance that permits the movement of electrically charged ions inside the cell. Depending on the cell, it may be a liquid, paste, gel or solid material.
  • Separator: In cells that use one, this prevents the electrodes from touching directly while allowing ionic conduction.
  • External circuit: Conducting wires and a connected device provide the path through which electrons transfer electrical energy to the device.

What are ions?

An ion is an atom or group of atoms carrying an electric charge. A positively charged ion is called a cation, while a negatively charged ion is called an anion. Ions help carry electric current through an electrolyte.

How a Cell Produces Current

Consider an electrochemical cell that is supplying electricity to a bulb. This condition is called discharging.

  1. A chemical reaction occurs at the negative electrode, releasing electrons. This electrode acts as the anode during discharge.
  2. When the external circuit is complete, electrons move from the negative terminal through the wire and connected bulb towards the positive terminal.
  3. At the positive electrode, another chemical reaction accepts electrons. This electrode acts as the cathode during discharge.
  4. Ions move within the electrolyte to maintain electrical balance and allow the reactions to continue.

The chemical process at the anode involves oxidation, meaning loss of electrons. The process at the cathode involves reduction, meaning gain of electrons. These complementary processes make electrical energy available to the external circuit.

Electron Flow and Conventional Current

During discharge, electrons move through the external metallic circuit from the negative terminal towards the positive terminal. However, the conventional direction of electric current is defined as the direction in which positive charge would move. Therefore, conventional current flows from positive to negative through the external circuit, opposite to electron flow.

Inside the cell, charge is carried mainly by ions rather than electrons travelling directly through the electrolyte.

When Does a Cell Stop Working?

A cell can supply current only while its chemical system can sustain the necessary reactions and maintain sufficient voltage. As discharge continues, the chemical composition of its active materials changes.

Eventually, the cell may no longer supply adequate voltage or current to the connected device. A primary cell must then be replaced, whereas a suitable rechargeable cell can be charged again.

A complete circuit is necessary for sustained current through an ordinary electrical device. Directly connecting the 2 terminals without a suitable load creates a short circuit, which may cause excessive current, heating and damage.

Prelims focus

  • An electrochemical cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy during discharge.
  • During discharge, the negative electrode is the anode and the positive electrode is the cathode.
  • Oxidation occurs at the anode; reduction occurs at the cathode.
  • Electrons travel through the external metallic circuit, while ions carry charge through the electrolyte.
  • Conventional current flows opposite to electron flow in the external circuit.
  • Trap: A battery does not generate energy from nothing; it converts stored chemical energy into electrical energy.

[NCERT, Science, Class 6, Chapter 12, Electricity and Circuits, Sections 12.1–12.3, printed pp. 116–119, 2018–19 edition; US Department of Energy, DOE Explains...Batteries, explanation of electrodes, electrolyte and energy conversion, consulted 3 November 2026.]

body:
Classification of Electric Cells

Electric cells are commonly classified according to whether their chemical reactions can be reversed sufficiently to restore their useful electrical capacity.

The 2 main categories are primary cells and secondary cells. Secondary cells are also called rechargeable cells or storage cells.

Primary Cells

A primary cell is an electrochemical cell intended for use until its available chemical energy is exhausted. It is not designed to be restored by ordinary electrical recharging.

In a primary cell, the chemical reactions during discharge are not practically reversible under the cell's intended operating conditions. Attempting to recharge a cell not designed for charging can cause leakage, overheating or other hazards.

Common Examples

  • Zinc-carbon dry cell: A familiar primary cell used in low-power devices such as torches, clocks and some remote controls.
  • Alkaline cell: Commonly used in remote controls, toys and portable devices. It generally offers better performance than a conventional zinc-carbon cell under many comparable conditions.
  • Primary lithium cell: Used in certain watches, cameras, memory-backup devices and other equipment requiring long storage life or particular operating characteristics.

A conventional dry cell is called dry because its electrolyte is held in a paste or other relatively immobilised form rather than as a freely flowing liquid. It is not completely free of moisture.

Secondary or Rechargeable Cells

A secondary cell is an electrochemical cell designed to undergo repeated discharge and recharge. An external electrical supply reverses the useful chemical changes sufficiently to restore its capacity.

When a rechargeable cell supplies electricity, it converts stored chemical energy into electrical energy. During charging, an external source supplies electrical energy, which is stored through chemical changes within the cell.

Important Rechargeable Battery Types

  • Lead-acid battery: Commonly used for starting conventional automobiles and for backup power systems such as inverters and uninterruptible power supplies. It uses lead-based electrodes and sulphuric acid electrolyte.
  • Lithium-ion battery: Widely used in mobile phones, laptops, rechargeable tools, electric vehicles and stationary energy-storage systems. During operation, lithium ions move within the cell between its electrodes.
  • Nickel-metal hydride battery: Used in certain rechargeable consumer cells and other applications. It is a secondary battery technology.

A lithium-ion battery should not be confused with a primary lithium-metal battery. Both involve lithium chemistry, but their construction and intended rechargeability differ.

Primary and Secondary Cells Compared

FeaturePrimary cellSecondary cell
RechargeabilityNot designed for normal rechargingDesigned for repeated recharging
Discharge reactionNot practically reversible for normal reuseSufficiently reversible for repeated use
ExamplesZinc-carbon, ordinary alkalineLead-acid, lithium-ion
Typical applicationLow-power, occasional-use devicesDevices requiring frequent energy replenishment
End of useful lifeReplaced after depletionReplaced after capacity or performance becomes inadequate

What Determines Battery Usefulness?

Voltage represents the electrical potential difference between the terminals. A common zinc-carbon or alkaline cylindrical cell has a nominal voltage of approximately 1.5 V.

When 2 such cells are connected correctly in series, their voltages add to approximately 3 V. Connecting cells in series increases the total voltage, but does not automatically make each cell store more energy.

Capacity indicates how much electrical charge a battery can deliver under specified conditions. The amount of useful energy also depends on voltage and operating conditions.

Different devices require different combinations of voltage, energy storage, size, weight, cost and service life. Lithium-ion batteries are useful in portable electronics because they can store comparatively large amounts of energy for their size and weight. Lead-acid batteries remain useful where their cost, availability and ability to deliver high starting currents are advantageous.

Rechargeable batteries do not last indefinitely. Repeated charging and discharging, temperature and operating conditions gradually affect their performance.

Important Classification Distinctions

The physical shape of a battery does not always reveal whether it is rechargeable. Cylindrical, rectangular and coin-shaped cells can exist in different chemistries. A cell should be classified by its chemistry and intended operation, not merely its appearance.

Also, a solar cell is different from a rechargeable electrochemical cell. A solar cell converts light directly into electricity through the photovoltaic effect, whereas an electrochemical storage cell relies on chemical reactions. A solar panel can charge a suitable battery through the appropriate electrical system, but the 2 devices perform different functions.

Prelims focus

  • Primary cells are not intended for ordinary electrical recharging.
  • Lead-acid and lithium-ion batteries are examples of secondary cells.
  • Conventional zinc-carbon and ordinary alkaline cells are primary cells.
  • A typical zinc-carbon or alkaline cylindrical cell supplies approximately 1.5 V nominal voltage.
  • Two 1.5 V cells connected correctly in series supply approximately 3 V.
  • Trap: A lithium-ion rechargeable cell is not the same as a primary lithium-metal cell.

[NCERT, Science, Class 6, Chapter 12, Electricity and Circuits, Sections 12.1–12.3; US Department of Energy, DOE Explains...Batteries, charging and discharging; US Environmental Protection Agency, Used Household Batteries and Used Lithium-Ion Batteries, sections on single-use and rechargeable batteries, consulted 3 November 2026.]

body:
Meaning of Electrolysis

Electricity can be produced by chemical reactions, but electricity can also be used to bring about chemical reactions. The second process is especially important in industrial chemistry.

Electrolysis is the process of using electrical energy to bring about a chemical change that requires an external electrical supply.

For example, electrical energy can be used to decompose water into hydrogen and oxygen or to deposit a metal coating on another material.

The apparatus in which electrolysis occurs is called an electrolytic cell.

Why an Electrolyte Is Necessary

An electrolyte contains mobile ions that carry electric charge through a liquid, molten substance or suitable solid medium.

In ordinary aqueous solutions, dissolved acids, bases and salts commonly provide ions that conduct electricity. However, different solutions have different electrical conductivities.

Conducting and Poorly Conducting Liquids

  • Salt solution: Common salt dissolved in water produces mobile ions, allowing current to pass.
  • Acidic solution: Lemon juice and vinegar contain acids that produce ions in water, enabling electrical conduction.
  • Basic solution: A suitable dissolved base, such as sodium hydroxide, produces ions and conducts electricity.
  • Distilled water: It contains very few dissolved ions and is therefore a poor conductor under ordinary school-level testing conditions.
  • Sugar solution: Sugar dissolves mainly as neutral molecules rather than producing a substantial concentration of ions. It is therefore a poor conductor compared with an ordinary salt solution.

Pure water is not a perfect electrical insulator because a very small concentration of ions exists naturally. Nevertheless, its conductivity is extremely low compared with water containing substantial dissolved electrolytes.

Tap water usually conducts electricity better than distilled water because it contains dissolved mineral salts. The exact conductivity depends on the substances dissolved in it.

Electrodes in an Electrolytic Cell

An ordinary electrolytic cell contains 2 electrodes connected to an external direct-current electrical supply.

  • Cathode: The electrode connected to the negative terminal of the external supply. Positive ions can move towards it and undergo reduction.
  • Anode: The electrode connected to the positive terminal of the external supply. Negative ions can move towards it and undergo oxidation.

The names anode and cathode refer to the types of reactions occurring at the electrodes, not to a permanently fixed electrical sign in every electrochemical system.

Electrolytic and Galvanic Cells Compared

FeatureDischarging galvanic cellElectrolytic cell
Energy conversionChemical to electricalElectrical to chemical
External power needed to drive the reactionNoYes
AnodeNegativePositive
CathodePositiveNegative
OxidationAt anodeAt anode
ReductionAt cathodeAt cathode

Anode means oxidation; cathode means reduction. These reaction definitions apply to both galvanic and electrolytic cells. The electrical signs differ because one system produces electrical energy while the other is driven by an external supply.

Electrolysis of Water

Water can be decomposed into hydrogen and oxygen using electrical energy. Under appropriate electrolysis conditions, with suitable electrodes and an electrolyte:

  • Hydrogen gas is produced at the negative electrode, or cathode.
  • Oxygen gas is produced at the positive electrode, or anode.

The volume of hydrogen obtained is approximately 2 times the volume of oxygen under the same temperature and pressure conditions. The hydrogen-to-oxygen volume ratio is therefore 2:1.

Water electrolysis requires electrical energy. It is therefore not an example of a battery spontaneously supplying electricity. The electrical input drives a chemical decomposition reaction.

The products also depend on the substances present in the electrolyte. For example, electrolysis of an aqueous sodium chloride solution can produce chlorine at the anode instead of oxygen. Consequently, it is incorrect to assume that every aqueous solution produces only hydrogen and oxygen during electrolysis.

Observable Chemical Effects of Electric Current

When current passes through a suitable conducting solution, chemical changes may produce visible effects:

  • Gas bubbles may appear near an electrode.
  • A metal may be deposited on an electrode or another conducting object.
  • The colour of the solution may change as substances are formed or consumed.
  • Materials at an electrode may dissolve or undergo another chemical change.

The precise result depends on the electrolyte, electrode materials and operating conditions. The passage of current does not necessarily produce the same reaction in every liquid.

Prelims focus

  • Electrolysis converts electrical energy into chemical change.
  • In an electrolytic cell, the anode is positive and the cathode is negative.
  • Oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode.
  • In suitable water electrolysis, hydrogen forms at the cathode and oxygen at the anode.
  • The hydrogen-to-oxygen volume ratio in water electrolysis is 2:1.
  • Trap: Pure water is a very poor conductor, while dissolved salts generally improve its conductivity.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 14, Chemical Effects of Electric Current, Sections 14.1–14.2, printed pp. 172–177, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 2, Acids, Bases and Salts, Section 2.4.3, p. 30, 2026–27 reprint; Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, National Green Hydrogen Mission information portal, Production Pathways and Technologies, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Electrolysis: Producing Chemical Changes with Electricity
